title: Query execution and planner
scopeHtml: Scope: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, scan and join algorithms, statistics, and common slow-query fixes.

notes.title: From SQL text to results: the pipeline
notes.html:
A query goes through parse, rewrite, plan, then execute. The parser checks syntax and names. The planner (optimizer) looks at many possible ways to run the query and picks the one with the lowest estimated cost. The executor runs that plan as a tree of nodes, each pulling rows from its children.

The planner is cost-based: it uses table statistics (row counts, value distributions) and cost constants (seq_page_cost 1.0, random_page_cost 4.0, cpu_tuple_cost 0.01 by default in Postgres) to estimate. Estimates can be wrong, and most slow queries are slow because of a wrong estimate or a missing index.

Worked example. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7: candidate plans are a sequential scan, an index scan, or a bitmap scan. With 50M rows and an estimated 100 matches, the index plan costs maybe 20 units versus 800,000 for the scan, so it picks the index.

Industry examples. Postgres, MySQL 8, Oracle and SQL Server all use cost-based optimisers. Newer systems (CockroachDB, Spanner) use the same idea distributed. Google's and Meta's engineers have written about estimation errors being the number one cause of bad plans.

Everyday analogy. A GPS comparing routes using estimated traffic. If the traffic data is stale, it picks a bad route confidently.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking the database runs your joins in the order you wrote them.
  • Forgetting that estimates (not truth) drive the plan.

notes.title: Reading EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
notes.html:
EXPLAIN shows the plan and estimates without running the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and adds actual times and row counts. Beware: ANALYZE really executes (wrap INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;).

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT c.name, sum(o.total)
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created >= '2025-05-01' GROUP BY c.name;
HashAggregate  (cost=2150.20..2160.20 rows=1000 width=40) (actual time=41.2..41.5 rows=980 loops=1)
  Group Key: c.name
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 193kB
  Buffers: shared hit=1450
  ->  Hash Join  (cost=290.00..2000.00 rows=20000 width=36) (actual time=3.1..30.8 rows=21345 loops=1)
        Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.00..1500.00 rows=20000 width=8) (actual time=0.02..15.2 rows=21345 loops=1)
              Filter: (created >= '2025-05-01'::date)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 78655
        ->  Hash  (cost=165.00..165.00 rows=10000 width=36) (actual time=3.0..3.0 rows=10000 loops=1)
              Buckets: 16384  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 720kB
              ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (cost=0.00..165.00 rows=10000 width=36)
Planning Time: 0.4 ms
Execution Time: 42.0 ms

How to read it:

  • The tree is read bottom-up, innermost first. Indentation shows parents and children.
  • cost=a..b: a = startup cost (before first row), b = total cost, in arbitrary units.
  • rows= estimated vs actual ... rows= real. A big gap (10x or more) is the first thing to hunt.
  • loops=N: the node ran N times; actual time and rows are PER LOOP, so multiply. A nested loop inner side with loops=100000 is a typical culprit.
  • Buffers: shared hit (cache) vs read (disk); Rows Removed by Filter shows wasted work.
  • Planning Time vs Execution Time.

MySQL equivalent. EXPLAIN shows a table with type (ALL = full scan, index, range, ref, eq_ref, const), key (index used), rows (estimate), Extra (Using index, Using filesort, Using temporary). EXPLAIN ANALYZE exists in 8.0.18+ and prints a tree like Postgres.

Worked example (spotting the problem). Plan says rows=20 estimated but actual rows=2,000,000. The planner picked a nested loop because it expected 20 inner iterations; reality made it 2M. Fix the estimate (ANALYZE, extended statistics) rather than forcing the plan.

Everyday analogy. An itinerary with predicted and actual times for each leg: the leg where the two disagree most is where your trip went wrong.

Common interview traps.

  • Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write without a rollback.
  • Ignoring loops.
  • Trusting cost numbers across different queries; they are only comparable within one planner.

notes.title: Scan types: seq, index, bitmap, index-only
notes.html:
The scan node says how rows are read from one table.

Node When it wins
Seq Scan Reading a large fraction of the table, or a tiny table
Index Scan Few rows, or needs index order (e.g. ORDER BY ... LIMIT)
Bitmap Index + Bitmap Heap Scan Medium number of rows: collects matching row locations, sorts them by page, reads each heap page once; can combine several indexes with AND/OR
Index Only Scan All needed columns are in the index (and visibility map is clean) 
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'paid';
--  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=12.4..560.0 rows=180 width=40) (actual time=0.15..0.9 rows=175 loops=1)
--    Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 7)
--    Filter: (status = 'paid'::text)
--    Heap Blocks: exact=160
--    ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_idx (cost=0.0..12.3 rows=200) (actual rows=200)
--          Index Cond: (customer_id = 7)

Why bitmap exists. Plain index scans on 5,000 matches would do 5,000 random heap reads, maybe hitting the same page many times. A bitmap sorts page numbers first, reads each once in physical order (closer to sequential). Recheck Cond appears when the bitmap becomes lossy (work_mem too small, shown as lossy= blocks).

Parallel scans. Postgres can use Parallel Seq Scan with workers (max_parallel_workers_per_gather, default 2) for large scans; Gather merges results. Good for analytics; avoid in high-QPS OLTP where it steals CPU.

Worked example. A table with 10M rows (80k pages): Seq scan cost ~ 80,000 pages x 1.0 + 10M x 0.01 = 180,000. A filter returning 1,000 rows via index: ~ 1,000 x 4.0 random + overhead = ~4,000 to 5,000. Index wins by ~40x. At 3M matching rows the index would cost ~12M units, and seq scan wins.

Everyday analogy. Collecting 200 books: first write down all shelf locations, sort the list, then walk the library once rather than zigzagging for every book.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking Seq Scan is always bad.
  • Not knowing what a bitmap scan is for.
  • Forgetting ORDER BY ... LIMIT can make an index scan win even for many matches (stops early).

notes.title: Join algorithms: nested loop, hash, merge
notes.html:
Three ways to join two inputs. The planner chooses by estimated sizes, available indexes, and sort order.

Nested loop. For each row of the outer side, look up matches in the inner side. Great when the outer is small and the inner has an index; terrible when both are large with no index (O(n x m)).

for each row o in orders_filtered (outer, 20 rows):
    index lookup customers where id = o.customer_id      (inner, ~0.01 ms)

Hash join. Build a hash table from the smaller input, then scan the larger one probing it. Cost O(n + m). Needs memory (work_mem, default 4 MB per hash operation in Postgres); if the build side doesn't fit, it splits into batches written to disk (Batches: 8 in EXPLAIN). Only for equality joins.

Merge join. Sort both inputs on the join key (or use an index that is already sorted) and walk them in step. Cost O(n log n + m log m), or O(n + m) if already sorted. Handles huge inputs without big hash memory; supports range/equality on sortable keys.

Nested loop Hash Merge
Best for Few outer rows, indexed inner Big equality joins Pre-sorted big inputs
Memory Tiny Hash table of smaller side Sort buffers
Starts returning rows Immediately After build phase After sorts

Worked example. Join 10k customers to 10M orders on customer_id.

  • Nested loop (customers outer, index on orders): 10k x ~0.03 ms = 300 ms.
  • Hash join (hash 10k customers ~1 MB, scan 10M orders): ~1 to 2 s with cold data, less cached.
  • If the customer filter reduces to 5 rows: nested loop becomes 0.2 ms. The right choice flips with row counts, which is why accurate estimates matter.

MySQL differences. Before 8.0.18 MySQL had only nested loop variants (plus block nested loop). 8.0.18 added hash join (used when there is no usable index). No merge join. This is why older MySQL schemas had to index every join column.

Join order. For many tables, join order explodes (n! orders). Postgres searches exhaustively up to join_collapse_limit (default 8) and from_collapse_limit (8), then uses a genetic optimiser (geqo_threshold 12). A 12-way join can get a poor plan.

Everyday analogy. Matching names from two lists: look each name up one by one (nested loop), put one list in a hash/lookup board (hash), or sort both lists and walk them together (merge).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying hash join is always fastest.
  • Not knowing that a join can spill to disk when work_mem is too small.
  • Assuming the order you write the joins is the executed order.

notes.title: Statistics and cardinality estimation
notes.html:
Statistics are the numbers the planner uses to guess how many rows each step returns. Postgres collects them with ANALYZE (autovacuum runs it automatically) into pg_statistic, viewable via pg_stats.

Per column it stores: null fraction, number of distinct values (n_distinct), most common values and their frequencies, a histogram of the rest, and correlation with physical order. Sample size is default_statistics_target (default 100, meaning about 30,000 sampled rows per table via 300 x target).

SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'status';
-- status | 0 | 4 | {paid,refunded,pending,failed} | {0.9,0.05,0.04,0.01}

With status = 'pending' the planner estimates 0.04 x total rows. For 50M rows: 2M. Simple and usually right.

Where estimates go wrong.

  • Correlated columns. WHERE city = 'Pune' AND pincode = '411001': the planner assumes independence and multiplies selectivities, underestimating wildly. Fix: extended statistics: CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies) ON city, pincode FROM addresses; ANALYZE addresses;
  • Stale stats after a bulk load: ANALYZE right after big loads or migrations.
  • Expression or function filters: no stats unless you create an expression index (which gets its own stats).
  • Skewed distributions with a big tail: raise the target for that column: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 1000; ANALYZE orders;
  • Joins across skewed keys.
  • Parameterised/prepared statements. After 5 executions Postgres may adopt a generic plan (plan_cache_mode auto) that ignores the specific parameter; a query that is fast for rare values and slow for the hot value (or vice versa) shows this; plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan can help.

Worked example. After loading 40M rows with COPY, autovacuum has not yet run; the planner thinks the table has 1,000 rows (old stats) and picks nested loops with seq scans inside. The query goes from 200 ms to 40 minutes. A manual ANALYZE fixes it in seconds. Metric to alert on: n_mod_since_analyze in pg_stat_user_tables.

MySQL. InnoDB uses persistent sampled statistics (innodb_stats_persistent, default on), refreshed by ANALYZE TABLE; MySQL 8 also supports histograms (ANALYZE TABLE t UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON col).

Industry examples. Postgres planner estimation blind spots (correlation) are a well-known cause of bad plans in production postmortems; teams respond with extended statistics, pg_hint_plan (an extension), or schema changes. Oracle and SQL Server give plan hints and adaptive plans more directly.

Everyday analogy. A survey sample used to estimate a city's population. A small, outdated or biased sample gives a confident wrong answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Telling someone to "force an index" before checking statistics.
  • Not running ANALYZE after bulk loads.
  • Ignoring column correlation.

notes.title: Common slow-query fixes
notes.html:
A debugging routine beats memorised tricks. Find the slow query (pg_stat_statements, slow query log, auto_explain), run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), find the node with the most time or biggest estimate gap, then pick the fix.

Fix catalogue:

  1. Seq scan on a big table with a selective filter: add the right (composite/partial) index.
  2. Function or cast on the column: rewrite the predicate or add an expression index.
  3. N+1 queries from the app: replace 1 + N queries with one join or WHERE id = ANY($1). 500 queries x 2 ms = 1 s of round trips versus one 5 ms query.
  4. Deep OFFSET: switch to keyset pagination.
  5. SELECT * on wide rows (large text/jsonb is TOASTed): select only needed columns to enable index-only scans and smaller transfers.
  6. Sort spilling to disk (Sort Method: external merge Disk: 120MB): add an index in the desired order, raise work_mem for that session, or reduce rows before sorting.
  7. Hash aggregate or join spilling: raise work_mem carefully (it is per operation per connection: 64 MB x 4 nodes x 200 connections = 51 GB).
  8. Correlated subquery run per row: rewrite as a join or EXISTS, ensure an index.
  9. COUNT(*) on large tables: Postgres has no free row count (MVCC); use estimates (reltuples), a maintained counter, or approximate; add filters + index-only scan.
  10. Lock waits, not CPU: EXPLAIN looks fine but the query waits; check pg_stat_activity.wait_event and pg_locks.
  11. Too many connections: use a pooler (PgBouncer); 500 connections cause context switching; target roughly 2 to 4 x CPU cores of active connections.

Example: sort spill.

Sort  (cost=...) (actual time=1850..2100 rows=2000000 loops=1)
  Sort Key: created DESC
  Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 187000kB

Fix: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created DESC) lets the plan read in order and apply LIMIT 50 after reading 50 rows (about 0.5 ms), removing the sort entirely.

Example: N+1.

-- App loop: 1 query for orders, then per order:  SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1;
-- One round trip instead:
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ANY ($1::int[]);

Worked example (production). An API endpoint p99 jumps from 80 ms to 4 s after a deploy. pg_stat_statements shows a new query dominating total_exec_time; the plan shows Nested Loop ... loops=250000 due to an underestimated join. After CREATE STATISTICS on the correlated columns and ANALYZE, the plan switches to a hash join: 90 ms.

Industry examples. GitHub, Shopify and Stripe engineering write-ups consistently find: missing/composite indexes, N+1 from ORMs, and stale/misleading statistics as the top three causes of slow queries. Tools: pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, pgBadger, MySQL performance_schema and slow query log with pt-query-digest.

Decision gravity. Query rewrites are reversible and local. Index and statistics changes are reversible but affect other queries. Query hints/plan forcing are fragile (data distribution changes); treat them as last resort and document them.

Everyday analogy. A mechanic: listen to where the noise is (measure), find the worn part (EXPLAIN), replace that one part (fix) and test-drive (re-measure) rather than replacing the whole engine.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising without measuring or checking the actual plan.
  • Raising work_mem globally to a huge value.
  • Treating every slow query as an indexing problem (could be locks, N+1, connection storm, or stale stats).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Pipeline: parse, plan (cost-based, uses statistics), execute. Estimates drive plans.
  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS): read bottom-up, compare estimated vs actual rows, watch loops, Rows Removed by Filter, Buffers, and disk spills; wrap writes in a rolled-back transaction.
  • Scan nodes: seq, index, bitmap, index-only; each wins at a different selectivity.
  • Join algorithms: nested loop (small outer, indexed inner), hash (big equality, needs work_mem), merge (sorted inputs); MySQL got hash join only in 8.0.18.
  • Statistics: ANALYZE after bulk loads, extended statistics for correlated columns, higher STATISTICS target for skew; alert on stale stats.
  • Slow-query routine: find, EXPLAIN, locate the bad node, fix (index, rewrite, keyset pagination, N+1, spill, stats), re-measure.
  • Prefer the least invasive fix; avoid plan forcing and giant global work_mem.

questions.promptHtml: What happens between sending a SQL string to Postgres and getting rows back?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know SQL is declarative and that the planner, not your text, picks the execution strategy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The server parses the text and resolves names, rewrites views and rules, then the planner enumerates ways to run it (scan types, join orders, join algorithms) and picks the cheapest by estimated cost. The executor then runs the chosen plan as a tree of nodes, each pulling rows from its children. The plan depends on statistics, so wrong estimates, not the SQL text, are the usual reason a query is slow.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SQL text -> Parser -> Rewriter -> Planner/Optimizer -> Plan tree -> Executor -> Rows
                                      ^ statistics + cost constants
  • Cost constants (defaults): seq_page_cost 1.0, random_page_cost 4.0, cpu_tuple_cost 0.01.
  • Candidate plans for WHERE customer_id = 7 on 50M rows: seq scan (~800k units), index scan (~20), bitmap scan. Cheapest wins.
  • Join order is not the order you wrote: the planner reorders inner joins (up to join_collapse_limit, default 8).
  • Plans are cached for prepared statements; after several executions Postgres may switch to a generic plan.
  • Estimates are not truth: cost numbers are only comparable within one planner run.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing joins run in the order you typed them.
  • Treating cost units as milliseconds.
  • Assuming the plan is stable when data distribution shifts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do the row estimates come from? -> pg_statistic (pg_stats): null fraction, n_distinct, MCVs, histogram, correlation.
  2. Why can the same SQL be fast then slow? -> Data growth, stale stats, parameter values, or a plan-cache switch to a generic plan.
  3. Can I force a plan? -> Not natively; only via settings (enable_*), CTE materialisation, or an extension like pg_hint_plan, all fragile.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "parse, plan, execute". Senior: cost model constants, statistics dependency, join reordering limits, plan caching and the consequence that most slow queries are estimation problems.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly bulk load left planner stats stale and queries went from 200 ms to 40 minutes until ANALYZE ran.

questions.promptHtml: How do you read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, and what do you look at first?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every performance interview reduces to plan literacy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I read the tree bottom-up, innermost node first. Then I compare estimated rows= with actual rows= on each node: a 10x or larger gap is where the planner went wrong. I multiply actual time and rows by loops, check Rows Removed by Filter, Buffers (hit vs read) and any Sort Method: external merge or Batches > 1 spill. EXPLAIN alone estimates; ANALYZE actually runs the query, so I wrap writes in BEGIN/ROLLBACK.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HashAggregate  (cost=2150..2160 rows=1000) (actual time=41.2..41.5 rows=980 loops=1)
  ->  Hash Join  (cost=290..2000 rows=20000) (actual time=3.1..30.8 rows=21345 loops=1)
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o (actual time=0.02..15.2 rows=21345)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 78655
        ->  Hash  (actual rows=10000)
              ->  Seq Scan on customers c
Planning Time: 0.4 ms   Execution Time: 42.0 ms
  • cost=a..b: startup and total in arbitrary units.
  • loops=N: actual time and rows are per loop; total = value x loops.
  • Buffers: shared hit=... read=...: cache vs disk.
  • Planning Time vs Execution Time: prepared statements amortise planning.
  • MySQL: type ALL/range/ref/eq_ref/const, key, rows, Extra; EXPLAIN ANALYZE since 8.0.18.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BEGIN;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) UPDATE orders SET status='x' WHERE id < 1000;
ROLLBACK;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on DELETE/UPDATE in production without ROLLBACK.
  • Ignoring loops and mis-sizing the cost of an inner nested-loop node.
  • Comparing cost numbers across different queries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does a big estimate gap tell you? -> Stale or insufficient stats, correlated predicates, or a generic plan.
  2. Why use BUFFERS? -> Separates CPU-bound from I/O-bound and shows cache effectiveness.
  3. Does EXPLAIN ANALYZE overhead matter? -> Per-node timing can add overhead (TIMING OFF to reduce it).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "look for seq scans". Senior: finds the estimate gap first, uses loops and buffers, and distinguishes slow-node vs wrong-plan problems.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An engineer ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE on production to "see the plan" and actually deleted rows.

questions.contextHtml:
An endpoint GET /orders returns 500 orders with items. It takes ~1.2 s; the DB CPU is 10% and each query in pg_stat_statements averages 0.9 ms. The ORM code:

orders = db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = %s LIMIT 500", [uid])
for o in orders:
    o.items = db.query("SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = %s", [o.id])

Network RTT to the DB is 1.5 ms. Red herring: the team wants to upgrade the instance size.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The DB is slow, add an index" or "upgrade the instance". The queries are individually fast; the number of them is the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there an index on order_items.order_id? How many items per order? Do we need all columns?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Batch the child fetch into one query with ANY.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N+1 queries (501 round trips x ~2.4 ms = ~1.2 s); missing index (unlikely given 0.9 ms); instance size (CPU is 10%, so no).
  4. How I'd verify: Count statements per request in the app log; pg_stat_statements.calls for the item query will be 500x the order query.
  5. Root cause: Round trips dominate, not DB work.
  6. Fix: One query for items, group in memory (or a join).
  7. Prevention: ORM eager-loading config, a per-request query-count assertion in tests, auto_explain plus logging of call counts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A big join duplicates the order columns per item; the ANY version transfers less. I would not upgrade hardware.
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ANY ($1::bigint[]);
-- needs: CREATE INDEX ON order_items (order_id);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if 100k ids? -> Chunk the array or use a join against a temp/VALUES list.
  • Is a JOIN always better? -> Not when parents have wide rows duplicated per child.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A list page made 2,000 queries per request; dropping to 3 reduced p99 from 4 s to 90 ms with zero DB changes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales the instance.
  • Hire: spots N+1 and batches.
  • Strong hire: quantifies RTT cost, verifies via call counts and adds guardrail tests.

questions.promptHtml: Compare seq scan, index scan, bitmap scan and index-only scan: when does each win and what is a bitmap scan for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand I/O patterns instead of "index good".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Seq scan reads everything sequentially and wins for large fractions or tiny tables. Index scan follows the index and does a random heap read per match, so it wins for few rows or when it supplies ORDER BY ... LIMIT. Bitmap scan is the middle: it collects matching row locations from the index, sorts them by heap page, and reads each page once, which is cheaper than many random reads and can AND/OR several indexes. Index-only scan skips the heap when the index has all columns and the visibility map allows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Index Scan:        idx -> heap page 5 -> idx -> heap page 91 -> idx -> heap page 5 (again)
Bitmap Heap Scan:  idx -> {5, 91, 5} -> sort/dedupe -> read page 5, then 91, once each
  • Recheck Cond and lossy blocks: when work_mem cannot hold the exact bitmap, it degrades to page-level and rechecks rows.
  • Parallel Seq Scan with Gather helps analytics; in high-QPS OLTP it steals CPU.
  • Illustrative cost: 10M rows (80k pages) seq ~180,000; 1,000 matches via index ~4,500; at 3M matches the seq scan wins.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'paid';
-- illustrative: Bitmap Heap Scan ... Heap Blocks: exact=160 -> Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_idx

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Seq scan is always bad."
  • Not knowing why a bitmap scan appears when you expected an index scan.
  • Forgetting that ORDER BY ... LIMIT can make an index scan win for many matches.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a bitmap scan lose index ordering? -> It reads in heap order, so a Sort is needed if ORDER BY is requested.
  2. What does lossy mean? -> Bitmap exceeded work_mem; entries collapse to pages and rows are rechecked.
  3. When is a Parallel Seq Scan bad? -> Many small concurrent queries; workers multiply CPU use.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names the four nodes. Senior explains the I/O pattern, thresholds, bitmap combining and lossy behaviour.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reporting query using a single index slowed when matches grew; the planner moved to a bitmap scan and the team learned why plans change with data size.

questions.subtopic: Estimate gap and nested loop explosion
questions.contextHtml:
After a Friday deploy, an API endpoint p99 jumps from 80 ms to 4 s. pg_stat_statements shows a new query dominating total_exec_time. Plan excerpt (illustrative):

Nested Loop  (cost=0.85..2400.10 rows=20 width=64) (actual time=0.1..3890 rows=250000 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using ads_campaign_idx on ads a (rows=20) (actual rows=250000 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (campaign_id = 9)
        Filter: (region = 'IN' AND city = 'Pune')
  ->  Index Scan using clicks_ad_idx on clicks c (rows=1) (actual time=0.01..0.015 rows=3 loops=250000)

The table was loaded last week by a backfill; autovacuum says "last_analyze: 9 days ago". Red herring: a recent index was added to clicks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more indexes" or "set enable_nestloop=off" globally. It ignores the 20 vs 250,000 estimate gap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in data (backfill)? Are region and city correlated? Do we have statistics targets customised?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run ANALYZE ads; (seconds, safe) and re-test; if the plan stays bad, a temporary per-query SET LOCAL enable_nestloop = off in the hot path while fixing properly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stale stats; (b) correlated predicates (city implies region) underestimated by multiplying selectivities; (c) generic prepared plan; (d) the new index (unlikely; nested loop already used an index).
  4. How I'd verify: Compare rows=20 with actual rows=250000; check pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze, n_mod_since_analyze; pg_stats for both columns.
  5. Root cause: The planner expected 20 outer rows, so nested loop with an index lookup looked ideal; with 250,000 outer rows the inner side runs 250,000 times.
  6. Fix: ANALYZE, then CREATE STATISTICS ads_loc (dependencies) ON region, city FROM ads; ANALYZE ads;. The plan flips to a hash join; here ~90 ms.
  7. Prevention: Alert on n_mod_since_analyze; ANALYZE after backfills in migration scripts; keep an eye on estimate-vs-actual ratios in auto_explain.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not force plans permanently; hints rot as data changes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• ANALYZE did not change the estimate? -> Correlated columns need extended statistics, not more sampling.
  • Estimates fixed but still slow? -> Check work_mem spills in the new hash join.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration copied 40M rows and nobody analyzed; the first nightly job ran 40 minutes; the fix was one ANALYZE line added to the runbook.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds indexes or disables nested loop globally.
  • Hire: reads the estimate gap and runs ANALYZE.
  • Strong hire: adds extended statistics, monitoring and runbook changes.

questions.contextHtml:
The admin "recent orders" page uses SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created DESC OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 50. orders has 40M rows. It takes 2.1 s and gets slower for deep pages. Plan (illustrative):

Limit (actual time=2080..2080 rows=50)
  ->  Sort (actual time=1850..2060 rows=100050)  Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 187000kB
        ->  Seq Scan on orders (actual rows=40000000)

Red herring: the DBA proposes raising work_mem to 1 GB globally.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raise work_mem globally or cache the page; ignores that OFFSET makes the DB produce and discard 100k rows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do users really jump to page 2,000? Is sort by created the only order? Is created unique?
  2. Immediate mitigation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON orders (created DESC, id DESC); so the plan reads in order and no sort is needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: No index in sort order (sort of 40M rows spilling); OFFSET discarding rows; work_mem low (symptom, not cause).
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN shows the Sort node disappears; Buffers falls.
  5. Root cause: OFFSET n must still produce n rows. Without an ordered index the DB sorts everything.
  6. Fix: Keyset pagination: WHERE (created, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50, passing the last row's values. Each page is ~0.5 ms regardless of depth.
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no OFFSET on large tables; API cursors instead of page numbers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keyset cannot jump to arbitrary pages; most UIs accept next/prev. I would not raise work_mem globally: 64 MB x several nodes x 200 connections = tens of GB.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_created_id_idx ON orders (created DESC, id DESC);
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The product needs "page 7,000 of 8,000"? -> Offer search/filters, or approximate with an indexed rank/bucket column.
  • Ties on created? -> Add id as tiebreaker, as above.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bot crawled ?page=N to 50,000 deep and saturated the primary; switching to cursors flattened latency.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises work_mem.
  • Hire: adds ordered index and keyset pagination.
  • Strong hire: explains OFFSET cost, tiebreakers and work_mem multiplication.

questions.promptHtml: Compare nested loop, hash join and merge join. When does the planner choose each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Join choice explains most plan-flip incidents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Nested loop probes the inner side for each outer row; it is best with a small outer and an indexed inner, and terrible for two large unindexed inputs. Hash join builds a hash table from the smaller side and probes it with the other: O(n+m), equality only, needs work_mem or it spills in batches. Merge join walks two sorted inputs together; good for large pre-sorted data and range-style comparisons on sortable keys. The choice flips with row counts, so accurate estimates matter.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Nested loop Hash Merge
Best for few outer rows, indexed inner large equality joins large sorted inputs
Memory tiny hash of smaller side sort buffers
First row immediately after build after sorts

Worked example (illustrative): 10k customers x 10M orders on customer_id. Nested loop with an index: 10k x ~0.03 ms = 300 ms. Hash: ~1 to 2 s cold. If the customer filter leaves 5 rows, nested loop is 0.2 ms.

  • Batches: 8 on a Hash node = spilled to disk.
  • MySQL: only nested-loop variants until 8.0.18 added hash join; no merge join.
  • Join order explodes factorially: Postgres searches exhaustively up to join_collapse_limit 8, GEQO at 12 tables.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.country = 'IN';

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Hash join is always fastest."
  • Not noticing a hash spill.
  • Assuming join order equals textual order.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why hash needs equality? -> Hash equality of keys; ranges and inequalities cannot be hashed.
  2. What makes merge join cheap? -> Inputs already sorted via index or earlier ORDER BY.
  3. How do you know a nested loop is dangerous? -> Inner node loops= in the hundreds of thousands with non-trivial time each.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions. Senior: cost drivers, memory behaviour, estimate sensitivity, MySQL differences and join-order limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A report flipped from hash join to nested loop after a stats change and ran 100x slower.

questions.contextHtml:
A reporting join of events (200M) to accounts (6M) runs in 90 s. Plan excerpt (illustrative):

Hash Join (actual time=21000..88000 rows=6000000 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on events ...
  ->  Hash (actual time=4100..4100 rows=6000000 loops=1)
        Buckets: 131072  Batches: 64  Memory Usage: 4096kB

work_mem is 4 MB. The primary also serves 300 OLTP connections. A teammate wants ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '1GB'.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Set work_mem huge globally, risking OOM; or force a different join type.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often is the report run? Can it run on a replica? How many concurrent reports? Server RAM?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Per-session setting for the report only: SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 64 batches means the hash table spills; the build side is 6M rows; alternatively pre-filter events earlier.
  4. How I'd verify: Re-run with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS); expect Batches: 1 and temp file reads gone (temp read/written in Buffers).
  5. Root cause: work_mem applies per operation per connection. Too small leads to batched spills (multiple passes over disk); too large risks 1 GB x nodes x connections exceeding RAM.
  6. Fix: Role-scoped setting for the reporting role (ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem='256MB'), run on a replica, reduce rows before joining (filter events by date), consider pre-aggregating.
  7. Prevention: Monitor temp_bytes in pg_stat_database; set log_temp_files.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set 1 GB globally: 1 GB x 4 nodes x 300 connections = 1.2 TB worst case. Also hash_mem_multiplier can raise hash limits specifically (verify version).
ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = '256MB';
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_temp_files = '50MB'; SELECT pg_reload_conf();

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Still spills at 256 MB? -> Reduce rows (filter, project fewer columns) or let it spill; or use merge join with sorted inputs.
  • What if the report runs concurrently 20x? -> Budget memory: 20 x ops x size must fit; use a queue.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A global work_mem bump during an incident caused OOM kills on Monday morning peak; per-role settings replaced it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: global 1 GB.
  • Hire: scopes setting per session or role.
  • Strong hire: calculates memory multiplication and reduces input rows.

questions.promptHtml: What statistics does Postgres keep, how are they used for row estimates, and what are their blind spots?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Estimation errors cause most bad plans; this shows you can fix them at the source.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ANALYZE samples the table and stores per-column null fraction, n_distinct, most common values with frequencies, a histogram of the rest, and physical correlation. The planner multiplies selectivities to estimate rows. It assumes columns are independent, so correlated predicates are underestimated; stale stats after bulk loads, expression filters and skew with a long tail also mislead it. Fixes: ANALYZE, extended statistics, higher per-column statistics target.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename='orders' AND attname='status';
-- illustrative: status | 0 | 4 | {paid,refunded,pending,failed} | {0.9,0.05,0.04,0.01}
  • status='pending': 0.04 x 50M = 2M rows estimated.
  • Sample size is about 300 x default_statistics_target (default 100) rows, so ~30,000.
  • Correlated columns: city='Pune' AND pincode='411001' multiplies two selectivities, underestimating; use CREATE STATISTICS s (dependencies) ON city, pincode FROM addresses.
  • Skew: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 1000;.
  • Expression/function filters have no stats unless an expression index exists.
  • MySQL: persistent sampled stats via ANALYZE TABLE; histograms in 8.0.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Force an index" before checking statistics.
  • Forgetting ANALYZE after COPY or migrations.
  • Ignoring column correlation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect stale stats? -> n_mod_since_analyze in pg_stat_user_tables, last_autoanalyze.
  2. Does raising the statistics target cost something? -> Slower ANALYZE and larger catalogs, plus slightly slower planning.
  3. How do prepared statements interfere? -> Generic plans ignore parameter values after ~5 executions, so MCV-based estimates can be lost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "run ANALYZE". Senior: knows the independence assumption, extended statistics, targets, expression stats and monitoring.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Correlated geo columns produced a 20-row estimate for 250,000 rows; extended statistics changed the plan from nested loop to hash join.

questions.contextHtml:
You are migrating 40M rows from a legacy table into new ledger_entries via INSERT ... SELECT in 500k batches while traffic stays live. After the cutover the dashboard query that took 200 ms now exceeds 40 minutes. Plan (illustrative):

Nested Loop (cost=0.00..8000.00 rows=10 width=48) (actual rows=3200000 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on ledger_entries l (rows=1000) (actual rows=40000000)
  ->  Index Scan on accounts a ... (loops=40000000)

pg_stat_user_tables: reltuples = 1000, n_mod_since_analyze = 40000000, last_autoanalyze is empty. Autovacuum is "running" on other big tables.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on, how do you recover, and how do you make the next migration safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blame the new code or add indexes; misses stats that say the table has 1,000 rows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are autovacuum workers saturated (autovacuum_max_workers)? Is the cutover reversible? Did any cancel the long query?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cancel the runaway query; run ANALYZE ledger_entries; manually. It samples ~30k rows and finishes in seconds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stats were never collected so the planner believes 1,000 rows; (b) autovacuum is busy elsewhere; (c) a missing index (check, but the nested loop makes sense only under the bad estimate).
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT reltuples, n_mod_since_analyze FROM pg_class JOIN pg_stat_user_tables ...; re-run EXPLAIN after ANALYZE and expect a hash join.
  5. Root cause: Autoanalyze triggers after a threshold of changes but lags; the planner used the empty-table estimate, choosing nested loop with a seq scan on the 40M row table.
  6. Fix: Immediate ANALYZE; add ANALYZE to the migration script after the load and before the cutover; consider per-table autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor for big tables.
  7. Prevention: Alert on n_mod_since_analyze / n_live_tup; migration checklist with "ANALYZE and compare plan on top 5 queries" before cutover.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on autovacuum timing for cutovers; running ANALYZE is cheap. I would not cancel via kill -9 on a backend.
INSERT INTO ledger_entries SELECT ... FROM legacy WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $2;
ANALYZE ledger_entries;
SELECT relname, n_mod_since_analyze, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='ledger_entries';

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partitioned table? -> Autovacuum does not analyze the partitioned parent; analyze it manually.
  • Does ANALYZE lock? -> It takes a light lock; safe on live tables.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "fast" cutover rehearsal on a loaded table hid this; production had no loaded stats and the first dashboard query ran for 20 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the query or adds indexes.
  • Hire: ANALYZE immediately.
  • Strong hire: root cause with reltuples/n_mod_since_analyze, plus migration and monitoring changes, including partitioned parent behaviour.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A service uses prepared statements through a driver: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT 20. One huge customer (customer_id = 1) has 18M of 60M rows; typical customers have 40. For two days, requests for the huge customer ran 12 s; a restart "fixed" it, then it returned. Observations (illustrative):

-- 6th execution onward
Index Scan Backward using orders_created_idx on orders (rows=20) -- filter customer_id = $1
   Rows Removed by Filter: 17,100,000

Red herring: a deploy occurred the same day.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened and what you change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the pool" or blame the deploy; no mention of plan caching.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Driver and server prepare thresholds? plan_cache_mode? Is a PgBouncer in transaction mode?
  2. Immediate mitigation: ALTER ROLE app SET plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan'; or the driver's prepareThreshold=0; connections pick it up on reconnect.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Generic plan chosen after ~5 executions based on average selectivity (customer rows ~40), picks the created-order index and filters; for the whale it scans 17M rows. Restart re-plans with custom plans for the first executions, hence the temporary fix.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) EXECUTE the prepared statement with the whale parameter; use auto_explain to capture the actual plan; check pg_prepared_statements.generic_plans.
  5. Root cause: The generic plan ignores the parameter's actual value, losing the MCV information that would reveal the skew.
  6. Fix: Force custom plans for this role/query, add composite index (customer_id, created DESC) so both cases are fast, and separate the whale in capacity planning.
  7. Prevention: Include skewed-parameter cases in load tests; auto_explain.log_analyze sampled in production; review checklist for prepared statements on skewed columns.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Custom plans cost planning time per call (~0.1 to 1 ms); acceptable here. I would not rely on restarts.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created DESC);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the composite index make both fast? -> It seeks on customer then reads in sort order, stopping after 20 entries regardless of the plan type.
  • Does PgBouncer matter? -> Transaction pooling plus server-side prepared statements needs care (verify version support).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single enterprise tenant made one query 300x slower than others; the real fix was the composite index, the setting only stopped the bleeding.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart-driven fixes.
  • Hire: knows generic plans and forces custom plan.
  • Strong hire: adds composite index, explains skew/MCV loss and prevention in tests.

questions.subtopic: Join order search and plan stability
questions.promptHtml: How does the planner choose join order for a 10-table query, and what goes wrong with many joins?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth: search space, thresholds and mitigation for ORM-generated mega-joins.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The number of join orders grows factorially, so Postgres does dynamic programming for up to join_collapse_limit/from_collapse_limit tables (default 8) and switches to the genetic optimiser GEQO at geqo_threshold 12, which is randomized and can return worse plans. Errors in each join's cardinality estimate compound multiplicatively, so large joins yield bad plans. Mitigations: simplify queries, split into steps/CTEs or temp tables with ANALYZE, and fix statistics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Inner joins can be reordered; outer joins have constraints. Beyond the collapse limit, the textual order of the remaining joins is kept as written.
  • Each estimate error multiplies: if each of 6 joins is 3x off, the last is 729x off.
  • Bushy plans (joining two intermediate results) are considered by the planner; the textual order only matters past the limits.
  • Techniques: materialize a selective sub-result into a temp table and ANALYZE it; use WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED to fence; raise join_collapse_limit carefully (planning time grows; check with EXPLAIN Planning Time).
  • MySQL uses a greedy search with optimizer_search_depth.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SET LOCAL join_collapse_limit = 12;   -- test planning time first
CREATE TEMP TABLE hot AS SELECT ... ; ANALYZE hot;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a 12-way ORM join gets an optimal plan.
  • Raising collapse limits globally and paying planning time on every query.
  • Not ANALYZE-ing temp tables, which have no stats.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do outer joins limit reordering? -> Reordering can change semantics, so only safe transformations are allowed.
  2. What does GEQO trade? -> Planning speed for plan quality and determinism.
  3. How to debug a bad many-join plan? -> Find the first node where estimate and actual diverge and fix statistics there.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "the planner picks the best order". Senior: search limits, compounding estimation error and practical decomposition.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An ORM-generated 14-table query flipped to a terrible plan when a table grew; splitting it into two steps fixed it.

questions.subtopic: Slow queries that are not plan problems
questions.contextHtml:
Support says "the app is slow sometimes, mostly around 14:00". The DB team looks: EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the reported query shows Execution Time: 3 ms. Yet the application times out at 5 s. pg_stat_activity at 14:02 (illustrative):

 state  | wait_event_type | wait_event    | count
 active | Lock            | transactionid | 112
 idle in transaction |    |               | 38
 active | IO              | DataFileRead  | 7

There are 480 connections to a 16-core server; the app has no pooler. A batch job runs at 14:00 updating 2M rows in one statement.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Query is fast, so it is the app", or adds indexes; misses locks and connection pressure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the exact endpoint and statement? Does the batch job share rows with the OLTP path? Are there idle in transaction sessions with open transactions holding locks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Identify the blocker with pg_blocking_pids(); terminate the offending session if safe; pause the batch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Row-lock queue behind the big UPDATE (112 waiting on transactionid); idle-in-transaction sessions pinning locks and the vacuum horizon; 480 connections thrashing on 16 cores; I/O (minor).
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), wait_event, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid))>0; and pg_locks; compare xact_start ages.
  5. Root cause: The plan is fine; the query waits. A single 2M-row transaction holds row locks for minutes, and connections stack up behind it.
  6. Fix: Chunk the batch (5k to 10k rows per transaction with commits), run it off-peak, set lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout='30s', and add PgBouncer sized to about 2 to 4 x cores of active connections.
  7. Prevention: Alert on wait_event_type='Lock' counts and longest transaction age; log lock waits (log_lock_waits).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add indexes or scale hardware; neither addresses waiting. Smaller batches take more wall-clock time but remove blocking.
SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS age, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blockers, wait_event, left(query,80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY age DESC;

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The blocker is idle in transaction from the app? -> Fix app code; timeout kills it.
  • Why is a 3 ms plan misleading? -> EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a quiet session does not reproduce lock waits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly "recalc" statement updating 3M rows made checkout time out at the top of the hour; chunking and a pooler removed the pattern.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: re-checks the plan only.
  • Hire: examines wait events and blocking.
  • Strong hire: chunks batches, adds timeouts and pooling, and sets alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A dashboard runs SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created >= date_trunc('day', now()) plus an overall SELECT count(*) FROM events for a header badge. events grew from 20M to 400M rows (expected 4B next year). The tenant count takes 80 ms; the global count takes 9 s and is called by every page load (300 req/s).

-- illustrative
Finalize Aggregate (actual time=9100..9100 rows=1)
  ->  Gather ... Parallel Seq Scan on events (actual rows=133000000 loops=3)

Red herring: someone suggests adding an index on id to speed up count.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do for the global count and the tenant count at 10x?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index" or "cache forever"; unaware that Postgres has no cheap exact count under MVCC.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the badge be exact? How stale can it be? Is the per-tenant number exact, and over what window?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the global count from the page-load path (cache for 60 s); stop parallel seq scans at 300 req/s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Exact count requires scanning visible rows (MVCC); index-only scan still checks visibility; the page-load frequency multiplies cost.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS); compare with SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname='events'.
  5. Root cause: Each transaction sees a different set of rows, so there is no stored exact count; counting means visiting rows or index entries.
  6. Fix: Global badge: use reltuples estimate or a maintained counter (trigger-free: a periodic job writing to a counters table). Tenant counts: index (tenant_id, created) so the query is an index-only range count (small per tenant), and a rollup table events_daily(tenant_id, day, n) updated by batch or stream. For approximate big counts, HyperLogLog (extension) where uniqueness is needed.
  7. Prevention: Reviews flag unbounded count(*) in request paths; budget per page load.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Counter tables risk hot-row contention if updated per event; use batched or sharded counters. I would not use triggers on a 4B table for a vanity metric.
SELECT reltuples::bigint AS approx FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'events';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY events_tenant_created ON events (tenant_id, created);

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Business requires exact tenant totals for billing? -> Compute from the ledger in a batch/rollup with checks, not on page load.
  • Parallel workers hurting OLTP? -> Lower max_parallel_workers_per_gather for the role.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "total users" badge issued a count on every page; after replacing it with a cached estimate, the primary's CPU dropped by a third.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: index on id.
  • Hire: estimate or cached counter, tenant index.
  • Strong hire: explains MVCC cost, rollups, contention trade-offs and request-path budgeting.
